title: The 90-Day Reporting Cost Calculator: What Your Weekly Status Decks Are Actually Costing You
subtitle: For owners and ops leads at 11-100 employee service firms. Three numbers in five minutes: labor cost, churn exposure, and 90-day recovery delta.

inputs.label: Active client accounts requiring weekly or bi-weekly reports
inputs.hint: Count every account that gets a recurring deliverable.

inputs.label: Average hours per report, per account, per week
inputs.hint: Include data pulling, formatting, QA, and the quick tweak the account lead makes before sending.

inputs.label: Fully-loaded hourly cost of the person doing reporting
inputs.hint: Salary + benefits + overhead ÷ 2,000. A $75k account manager is roughly $52/hr loaded.

inputs.label: Percentage of reports that arrive late or get skipped in a given month
inputs.hint: Be honest. 'We always send them' usually means 75-85% on time, not 100%.

inputs.label: Average monthly revenue per account
inputs.hint: Your typical retainer or recurring fee.

inputs.label: Average client tenure in months
inputs.hint: How long does a typical account stay before churning.

inputs.label: Churn lift when reporting is inconsistent
inputs.hint: Default 18% from service-firm churn audits. Inconsistent reporting is the #2 cited reason behind 'results weren't clear.'

inputs.label: Target reporting time per account after automation
inputs.hint: Most automated reporting flows land between 0.25 and 0.75 hours per account per week, including human review.

inputs.label: Expected build investment for the automation
inputs.hint: What you'd budget for the reporting automation build itself.

tier_thresholds.high_label: Critical — an FTE you haven't named

recommendations.text: You're in the manageable tier. Reporting is a cost, not a leak yet. Document the current flow end-to-end before scaling. Make sure the manual version is stable before you wire automation on top of it. Premature automation locks in a broken process.

You're in the compounding tier. The reporting layer is starting to eat capacity, and you'll feel it most past 10 accounts or when you try to hire your way out. Audit the 7 handoff points in your reporting workflow. Start with one automation: the data pull and template assembly. Keep human review on the narrative.

You're in the critical tier. Reporting is now a full-time hire you never put on the org chart, and the churn exposure is real, not theoretical. Run a full reporting automation pass within the next quarter. Target: drop per-account hours by 75%+ while keeping human review on every send. This is where the 90-Day Payback Rule kicks in hardest.

Your build pays for itself inside 90 days at the inputs above. That's the bar I use before greenlighting any automation project. If the math holds when you stress-test the inputs, this is a build, not a debate.

At these inputs the build doesn't clear payback inside 90 days. Two options: narrow the scope (automate the data pull only, not the full report), or wait until your account count or hours-per-report grows. Don't force a build whose math doesn't work.

You'd recover between half and one full FTE of capacity. The question becomes what you redeploy that time to — strategy work, new account onboarding, or pulling forward retainer expansions. The recovered hours are the asset; the automation is just how you get them.

capture_cta.headline: If your Total Annualized Exposure cleared $80,000, send me your inputs
